items.title: Earl Humphrey Interview, 1963-03-23
items.q: Leroy Evans was just the same way. Dead explosions and everything like that, we all worked together.

ctx.x: But when he's bucking somebody, what number would he play? Did he have a real crip that he could beat him with? Oh, he played.

I'm going to tell you, man, that guy, he was a good first-style guy. He played sweet numbers. He stayed at now. Oh, he had something to run him with now. Yeah, man. He could play the blues better than any trumpet playing time. Lee Cowden was a blues player. But he could take that mute, the rubber, you know, that flushing. Mm-hmm. When he get that thing up, he'd stand up in that truck. He'd go on there. Going back home to Jamaica, now he could play that. Mm-hmm. He had lots of numbers, man, he could play. That was…
Yeah, oh yeah, well he's still, he's a clock still.

items.title: Earl Humphrey Interview, 1963-03-28
items.q: We all worked together. ... We had good battery. Jesse, Cesar, Elisgar, Leroy.

ctx.x: He had lots of numbers, man, he could play. That lot of numbers. And then we had one of the best timekeepers, I mean beaters, Leroy Evans. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. He could take after Alfred. See, you know how Alfred keeps up story time? I haven't heard him play yet.
Yeah, oh yeah, well he's still, he's a clock still.
